sentence: Compact instruction-tuned language models are commonly deployed quantized, yet their safety is typically validated on the full-precision release.
cited: No — no citation marker is attached to this sentence (the extracted abstract carries no bracketed citations at all).
why_unsupported: Two independent prevalence claims in one sentence. "commonly deployed quantized" asserts real-world deployment frequency/market practice, which nothing in the reference list establishes — the model-release papers (Qwen3, Llama 3, Phi-4-Mini, Mistral 7B) establish capability, size and availability, not integration or deployment share, and the quantization-method papers (AWQ, GPTQ, QLoRA, LLM.int8) establish that methods exist and work, not that deployments routinely use them. "typically validated on the full-precision release" is a second prevalence claim, this time about the norms of the whole safety-evaluation literature, and would require a survey of release/safety-card practice that the report does not have. This is the exact wording ("commonly deployed quantized") that prior audits flagged, so it is a live regression, not a new phrasing.
proposed_fix: Replace with a capability/motivation framing that does not quantify practice: "Quantization makes compact instruction-tuned language models cheap enough to run on constrained hardware, but published safety evaluations are generally reported for the full-precision release, so the quantized artefact is not the artefact that was safety-tested." If a frequency claim is wanted, it must cite a deployment survey or telemetry source; absent one, drop "commonly" and "typically".

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTATION FAILED — the finding is real. All four refutation routes were tested and all fail.

(1) Not about the study's own data/design: the sentence makes two claims about the external world — deployment practice ("commonly deployed quantized") and the norms of the safety-evaluation literature ("typically validated on the full-precision release"). Neither is a property of this study's design, pairs, or benchmarks.

(2) Not scoped/hedged by surrounding context — the context aggravates it. Chapter 1 of the SAME swept snapshot (sweep/01_chapter_1_introduction.txt) states explicitly: "How often an end user in fact receives a quantized rather than a full-precision checkpoint is not something this study measures, and no prevalence figure is claimed for it." The Abstract asserts exactly the prevalence the body disclaims, so the report is internally inconsistent rather than scoped. The adverbs "commonly"/"typically" soften magnitude but remain frequency assertions.

(3) No citation supports it: the Abstract contains ZERO bracketed citations (grep -o "\[[0-9]\+\]" on 00_abstract.txt returns nothing). The auditor's reading of the reference list is correct — model-release papers [Qwen3, Llama 3, Phi-4-Mini, Mistral 7B] establish capability/size/availability; method papers [AWQ, GPTQ, QLoRA, LLM.int8] establish the methods work. Nothing in 11_references.txt measures deployment share or surveys release-time safety-validation practice.

(4) Not a definition — both halves are empirical prevalence claims.

sentence: Refusal-counting therefore overstates quantization harm.
cited: No — no citation marker attached.
why_unsupported: Generalises the same single-regex, single-benchmark observation into a standing claim about refusal-counting as a methodology and about "quantization harm" as a general quantity. The measured scope is: on HarmBench, at the 512-token budget, for these five pairs, the regex proxy attributed larger ASR increases to NF4 than the classifier did. It says nothing about refusal-counting under other quantization methods, other benchmarks, other model families, or other regex implementations.
proposed_fix: "Refusal-counting therefore overstated the apparent harm from quantization in this study's HarmBench contrasts."

verdict.reasoning:
I attempted to refute this and could not. Each of the four offered refutation routes fails, and the study's own primary artifact supplies counterexamples.

ROUTE 1 — "it is about the study's own data/design." Partially true but insufficient, and the report itself shows the authors intend the general reading. The parallel sentence in Chapter 1 (01_chapter_1_introduction.txt:57) is the same clause plus an explicit extension: "Refusal-counting therefore overstates quantization harm, and that is a cautionary lesson for safety evaluation generally." That is an author-declared generalisation from one regex on one benchmark to safety evaluation as a field — precisely the (b) pattern, not a compressed report of in-study data.

ROUTE 2 — "already adequately hedged and scoped." It is not. Unlike its neighbours, the sentence carries no scope qualifier at all: not the benchmark (HarmBench only; the classifier does not cover XSTest), not the precision (NF4), not the token budget (512), not the model set, not the regex implementation. The preceding sentence is a kappa figure and the following sentence is a paragraph break; the next paragraph's scoping ("Under the classifier at the 512-token reference budget, the study's primary configuration") governs the results claim, not the scorer claim. Contrast the same abstract's closing sentence, which does carry a scope ("...of four-bit quantization in small models"). Both terms are generalised: "Refusal-counting" as a methodology rather than "this v2 regex," and "quantization harm" as a quantity rather than "the NF4 HarmBench delta-ASR."

ROUTE 3 — "a citation establishes the proposition." No citation is attached, and nothing in 11_references.txt establishes a general property of refusal-counting under quantization.

ROUTE 4 — "it is a definition." No. It is an empirical directional claim about a measured quantity.

The decisive point is that the claim is not supported even within the study's own five pairs, on the exact quantity it names. From /Users/tanueihorng/fyp_quant/results_512/analysis/judge_agreement.json (per_pair, v2 delta vs judge delta): qwen_2b -0.025 vs 0.000; qwen_4b +0.070 vs +0.040; llama_3_2_3b -0.020 vs -0.040; mistral_7b +0.060 vs -0.020; phi4_mini 0.000 vs +0.020. The regex attributes MORE quantization harm in 3 of 5 pairs and LESS in 2 of 5 (qwen_2b and phi4_mini, where the judge delta exceeds the regex delta). The report's own labels confirm it: under the regex phi4_mini reads robust_preservation while the judge reads alignment_degradation — there the regex made quantization look safer, not harsher. The well-supported result is over-counting of the LEVEL of harmful compliance (judge_harmful_v2_not is ~0, a near-strict-superset relation, corroborated against human labels at kappa 0.59 vs 0.11). Over-counting the level does not entail over-stating the paired DELTA, and the paper's own numbers show it does not.

Notably the body states the correctly scoped version and the abstract does not. Section 6.9 (06_chapter_6_results_and_analysis.txt:779) says the two scorers "lead to different per-model conclusions about where, and in which direction, harmful compliance moves" — direction-agnostic and exactly right. Chapter 10 says "what determines the conclusion is the choice of scorer." The abstract sentence upgrades that symmetric, level-based, in-study finding into a one-directional standing law about a delta.

Per the repo's own D56 guidance (prefer the fix that adds rigour over deletion), the honest repair is wording the body already uses, e.g. "Refusal-counting therefore over-counts harmful compliance and changes which pairs look least safe" — fully supported by Table 6.3, the superset structure and the human-label audit, without asserting a uniform direction the data contradicts. The same edit should be applied to the Chapter 1 instance, where the "cautionary lesson ... generally" clause should be marked as an inference rather than a result.

Finding stands.

sentence: This regime corresponds to the practical envelope of contemporary on-device deployment.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: Asserts that the 1.7-7.2B band is what is actually deployed on device today. The study selected this band for tractability and hardware reasons; it measures nothing about deployment practice, and no source is offered for the envelope.
proposed_fix: State the selection rationale instead: "This regime was chosen because models of this size can be loaded and evaluated on a single 32 GB GPU and are the sizes released for on-device use by their publishers [2], [3]."

verdict.reasoning:
I tried all four refutation routes and none of them survives contact with the text.

**(1) "It's about the study's own design, not the world."** Fails. The sentence sits in §1.4 under "Model regime," and the three sentences before it *are* pure design statements ("The primary matched pairs sit in the roughly two-to-four-billion-parameter range... so the study spans approximately 1.7 to 7.2 billion parameters"). The target sentence then pivots outward and predicates something of the world — what "contemporary on-device deployment" practically encompasses. A rationale sentence that justifies a scope choice with a world-claim still asserts the world-claim. The study measures nothing about deployment practice.

**(2) "A citation on that sentence establishes it."** Fails. Confirmed at the source: `scripts/build_fyp_report_v6.js:424` renders the bullet with no bracket at all, while its immediate neighbours in the same chapter carry [1]–[6]. The string is verbatim unchanged since `scripts/build_fyp_report.js:355` (v1), i.e. it predates the citation-hardening pass that annotated the rest of Chapter 1. It is a legacy assertion that the hardening pass skipped.

**(3) "The surrounding context scopes it."** Fails, and in fact the context cuts the other way. §1.1 grounds only that "the smallest members of these families are sized for consumer hardware, mobile chipsets, and edge accelerators [2], [3]" and that quantization frameworks target edge inference [5]. Neither establishes an *envelope* — a bounded band identified with current on-device deployment. The band doesn't hold at either end on the report's own citations: [2] is Llama-3.2 including the 1B Instruct, below the study's 1.7B floor, so 1.7–7.2B does not bound the on-device space from below either. §2.3 likewise supports "below four billion... positioned for deployment at practical, resource-constrained scale" — it says nothing putting 7.2B in the envelope.

**(4) "It's a definition, or adequately hedged."** Fails. "Corresponds to **the** practical envelope of **contemporary** on-device deployment" is definite, present-tense, and unhedged — no "broadly," "approximately," "is commonly described as." It defines nothing; it asserts a correspondence between an empirically-chosen band and a real-world regime.

The decisive point is the report's own internal standard. Twice — §1.1 ("How often an end user in fact receives a quantized rather than a full-precision checkpoint is not something this study measures, and no prevalence figure is claimed for it") and §2.3 ("How widely each path is used in practice is not measured here, and no prevalence figure is claimed for it") — the author explicitly disclaims exactly this genre of deployment-practice claim. The band's upper bound was in fact set by what the cross-family extension reached (Mistral-7B, chosen to fit the TC1 6h/10GB envelope), so the sentence has the post-hoc structure the auditor names: a range fixed by tractability, re-described as a fact about the world.

Per D56 ("prefer the fix that adds rigour"), the fix is a reword plus citation rather than deletion, e.g. "This regime is the one that compression research targets for on-device inference [5], [7]" (which §1.1 already establishes), or an explicit hedge plus the same prevalence disclaimer already used in §1.1 and §2.3. sentence: The effect is also not bit-width-graded, in that a 128-token apparent increase in the smallest model does not replicate at the reference budget (Section 6.12).
defect_class: (f) absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence (with a supporting clause that does not support it)
cited: Internal cross-reference to Section 6.12; no external citation.
why_unsupported: Two problems. (i) "is not bit-width-graded" asserts the absence of a gradient; the study reports non-significant contrasts, which licenses "no bit-width gradient was detected", not that none exists — unless an equivalence test is quoted. (ii) The justification given varies the *generation-token budget* (128 vs 512), not the bit width, so it cannot bear on bit-width grading at all; the fp16 -> INT8 -> NF4 comparison is the relevant evidence and is not the one cited here.
proposed_fix: Separate the two claims and hedge the null: "No bit-width gradient is detected across fp16, INT8 and NF4 (Section 6.11). Separately, the 128-token apparent increase in the smallest model does not replicate at the 512-token reference budget (Section 6.12)."

verdict.reasoning:
I attempted refutation on all four permitted grounds and each fails.

**The warrant clause cites the wrong experiment (the auditor's prong (ii) is objectively correct).** I read both sections. §6.11 ("INT8 Precision Point: Method- and Bit-Width Sensitivity, fp16 to INT8 to NF4") is the ONLY place bit width is varied, and it is not the section cited. §6.12 is titled "Generation-Length Robustness: the 512-Token Rerun" and varies max_new_tokens only. The "128-token apparent increase in the smallest model" is Qwen3-1.7B's NF4 ΔASR +0.055 → 0.000 (Table 6.5), a single pair at a single bit width whose collapse is attributed to truncation ("roughly 60% of all responses were provably cut off"). That fact cannot bear on whether degradation is graded across fp16 → INT8 → NF4. The mismatch is confirmed by the report's own careful phrasing everywhere else, which keeps two conjuncts paired with two separate evidence streams: §6.11 concludes "neither bit-width-graded nor budget-robust" immediately after the INT8 nulls; Ch. 9 writes "neither bit-width-graded nor stable across generation budgets" after the INT8 evidence. The Introduction compressed this, kept conjunct 1 (bit width) and evidence stream 2 (budget), and welded them with "in that". Supplying a specific wrong warrant is worse than supplying none, because it misdirects a verifier.

A charitable rescue also fails on the facts: the 128-token signal that was INT8-specific and non-monotonic (rose at INT8, reverted at NF4 — the actual bit-width-grading evidence) belongs to **Llama-3.2-3B**, not the smallest model (§6.11, Appendix I.11). So the sentence cannot be read as a garbled reference to the INT8 result either — wrong model and wrong section.

**"Adequately hedged" fails, and the report itself proves the standard (prong (i)).** "The effect is also not bit-width-graded" is flat and unhedged. §6.11 explicitly states the correct epistemic rule — "Absence of significance is not by itself evidence of equivalence, so the same ten contrasts were also submitted to a two-one-sided-tests (TOST) equivalence procedure [49]" — but that TOST covers **capability only**. On the safety axis there is no equivalence test; Ch. 8 concedes the safety null is MDE-bounded at 0.04–0.09 ΔASR and "should therefore be read as bounded... rather than showing that the change is exactly zero." So the assertive "is not" wording on the safety axis is exactly the move the report disallows one section earlier, minus the TOST that licensed it there.

**"About the study's own data/design" does not save it.** That refutation applies when an auditor mistakes an internal result for a world-claim. Here the defect is internal warrant-to-claim mismatch, which survives it — and the sentence sits in the §1.5 Contributions list, where it reads as a general finding about quantization.

Fix that adds rigour rather than deleting (per D56): split the conjuncts and attach each to its own evidence, e.g. "No bit-width gradient was detected: every INT8 harmful-compliance contrast is non-significant under both judges across all five pairs (Section 6.11). Nor is the effect budget-robust — a 128-token apparent increase in the smallest model does not replicate at the reference budget (Section 6.12)." Optionally note that the safety null is bounded by the per-pair MDE, since no TOST was run on that axis.

sentence: First, baseline safety profiles differ substantially between families even at matched factual capability, so calibration is a property of the release rather than of model size.

I tried each refutation route and none holds.

1) "It's about the study's own data." Only the first clause is. "Baseline safety profiles differ substantially between families even at matched factual capability" is a clean description of the study's measurements (Llama-3.2-3B judge baseline ASR 0.100 vs Qwen3-1.7B 0.255 at MMLU 0.610 vs 0.643; 06_chapter_6 lines 603, 499). The "so ..." clause is not a description — it is an attributional decomposition ("property of the release", "rather than of model size") over factors the design never separates.

2) "Already hedged/scoped." There is no hedge; "is a property of X rather than Y" is flat. The scoping that IS present ("Four findings hold across the original three pairs") makes the second half worse, not better. Within those three pairs the baseline judge ASRs order monotonically by parameter count — 1.7B → 0.255, 3B → 0.100, 4B → 0.115 (lines 33, 173, 103) — i.e. the scoped evidence is fully consistent with a size effect. Worse, the report itself reads the one within-family size manipulation it has as exactly a size effect on calibration: line 499, "within the Qwen family the larger model is both more capable and more refusal-calibrated ... scaling from 1.7B to 4B reduces genuine baseline harmful compliance by 14.0 percentage points", and line 513, "quantization effects must be interpreted against scale-dependent baselines". §6.8 therefore contradicts §6.2/§6.2.1 of the same chapter. The auditor's line-499 citation checks out verbatim.

3) The stated premise does not support the stated conclusion. "Even at matched factual capability" controls MMLU, not parameters: the two models being compared (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen3-1.7B) differ in size by ~1.8x. Matched capability is not matched size, so nothing in the comparison licenses "rather than of model size". And with one release per family (Qwen the only family with two sizes), release, architecture, training corpus, alignment recipe and size are mutually confounded — "the release rather than the size" is a decomposition this design cannot perform. Alignment recipe is never varied or measured.

4) No citation is attached to the sentence, and nothing in 11_references.txt is invoked here; it is not a definition either.

Charitable reading considered and rejected as sufficient: "property of the release" could be meant as "you must check the specific checkpoint rather than infer from parameter count" (the report uses "release" to mean the released checkpoint elsewhere, e.g. ch.7 lines 15, 47). Even under that reading the "rather than of model size" half remains an unsupported negative claim that the study's own within-Qwen 14.0 pp result cuts against.

Note in fairness: the five-pair set does contain a genuine counterexample to a simple size law — Mistral-7B, the largest model at 7.2B, has by far the highest baseline judge ASR, 0.585 (line 631) — but that datum sits outside the sentence's own three-pair scope, is not invoked, and still cannot separate release from family/architecture.

A minimal fix that keeps the true content: "...differ substantially between families even at matched factual capability, so baseline calibration cannot be read off parameter count alone; family, alignment recipe and size co-vary in this design and are not separable here."
